scenes.visual: Title card 'Isolation Follows Ecology' over three small lakes seen from above, each with one OLIVE fish near the bottom and one SILVER-BLUE fish in open water. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP. COLOUR MAP (shared by both films, the take-homes and the lesson): M. lewisii always PINK flowers with a fuzzy BUMBLEBEE; M. cardinalis always RED tubular flowers with a HUMMINGBIRD; gene flow = a stream of small GOLD dots; each barrier = a GREY gate with its strength printed on it; a vertical DASHED line labelled 'zygote' sits right after the fertilization gate and separates prezygotic gates (left) from postzygotic gates (right); benthic stickleback OLIVE and deep-bodied, limnetic stickleback SILVER-BLUE and slender. All numbers appear only as on-screen text. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: If barriers are side effects of adapting to different habitats, isolation should follow the habitat. So what happens when fish adapted to the same habitat, but from different lakes, meet?
scenes.visual: Two OLIVE fish from two different lakes swim toward each other in a tank; a question mark between them.
scenes.narration: If barriers are side effects of adapting to different habitats, isolation should follow the habitat. So what happens when fish adapted to the same habitat, but from different lakes, meet?

scenes.tts: In the monkeyflowers, the strongest early gates were habitat and pollinators. Were those gates built to keep the species apart? Or did they come free with adaptation?
scenes.visual: Brief replay of the first film's row of GREY gates with the GOLD stream thinning; the 'habitat (ecogeographic)' and 'pollinator' gates glow, each with a question mark.
scenes.narration: In the monkeyflowers, the strongest early gates were habitat and pollinators. Were those gates built to keep the species apart? Or did they come free with adaptation?

scenes.tts: One answer is divergent selection, which favours different traits in different places. Two populations adapt to different habitats, and mating between them falls as a side effect.
scenes.visual: One population of fish splits into two groups heading to different habitats, bottom and open water. Arrows labelled 'divergent selection'. Between the two groups, the GOLD gene-flow stream thins.
scenes.narration: One answer is divergent selection, which favours different traits in different places. Two populations adapt to different habitats, and mating between them falls as a side effect.

scenes.tts: No one designs the barrier. Selection acts on individuals, and isolation appears along the way. Isolation that arises like this is called ecological speciation.
scenes.visual: A GREY gate assembles itself piece by piece in the stream, unattended, as the two groups adapt. Label: 'ecological speciation: isolation as a by-product of adaptation'.
scenes.narration: No one designs the barrier. Selection acts on individuals, and isolation appears along the way. Isolation that arises like this is called ecological speciation.

scenes.tts: How could you test it? Use evolution that repeated itself. Several small lakes in British Columbia each hold two forms of threespine stickleback.
scenes.visual: Map outline labelled 'British Columbia (schematic)'; three small lakes light up in turn, labelled 'lake A', 'lake B', 'lake C'.
scenes.narration: How could you test it? Use evolution that repeated itself. Several small lakes in British Columbia each hold two forms of threespine stickleback.

scenes.tts: The benthic form feeds on the bottom. The limnetic form feeds in open water. Each lake's pair is thought to have arisen on its own.
scenes.visual: Inside each lake: an OLIVE deep-bodied fish labelled 'benthic' near the lake bottom, a SILVER-BLUE slender fish labelled 'limnetic' in open water. In each lake a small arrow from one ancestor splits into the two forms, three separate splits. Body shapes are schematic.
scenes.narration: The benthic form feeds on the bottom. The limnetic form feeds in open water. Each lake's pair is thought to have arisen on its own.

scenes.tts: Rundle, Schluter and colleagues ran hundreds of laboratory mating trials, with fish from three lakes. They paired fish of the same and different forms, from the same and different lakes.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Rundle, Nagel, Boughman & Schluter, 2000'. An empty 2 by 2 grid: rows 'same form / different form', columns 'same lake / different lakes'. Small tank icons fill the margin; counter '750+ trials'.
scenes.narration: Rundle, Schluter and colleagues ran hundreds of laboratory mating trials, with fish from three lakes. They paired fish of the same and different forms, from the same and different lakes.

scenes.tts: A benthic fish from one lake meets a benthic fish from another lake. Their ancestors split apart separately. Will they mate?
scenes.visual: The 'same form, different lakes' cell is outlined; two OLIVE fish from lake A and lake B face each other. A question card.
scenes.narration: A benthic fish from one lake meets a benthic fish from another lake. Their ancestors split apart separately. Will they mate?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card holds; a 5-second ring timer counts down.

scenes.tts: Yes. Same-form pairs from different lakes showed no strong isolation. But benthic and limnetic fish were strongly isolated, whichever lakes they came from.
scenes.visual: Grid cells light up: both 'same form' cells bright (pairs spawning); both 'different form' cells dark, an OLIVE and a SILVER-BLUE fish turning away. Label: 'isolation tracks form, not lake'. Brightness is schematic.
scenes.narration: Yes. Same-form pairs from different lakes showed no strong isolation. But benthic and limnetic fish were strongly isolated, whichever lakes they came from.

scenes.tts: Look at what each idea predicted. If ancestry mattered, fish from one lake would mate best. If ecology mattered, fish of one form would mate best, wherever they came from.
scenes.visual: Two cards slide in over the lit grid. Card 'ancestry predicts': the 'same lake' column glows. Card 'ecology predicts': the 'same form' row glows. The ecology card's pattern matches the lit grid and gets a tick; the ancestry card fades.
scenes.narration: Look at what each idea predicted. If ancestry mattered, fish from one lake would mate best. If ecology mattered, fish of one form would mate best, wherever they came from.

scenes.tts: So isolation followed ecology, not ancestry. Drift alone would be unlikely to repeat the same pattern lake after lake. Divergent selection is the likely cause.
scenes.visual: The three lakes again; in each, a GREY gate appears between OLIVE and SILVER-BLUE fish, the same gate three times. Label: 'repeats with the environment → divergent selection (likely cause)'.
scenes.narration: So isolation followed ecology, not ancestry. Drift alone would be unlikely to repeat the same pattern lake after lake. Divergent selection is the likely cause.

scenes.tts: Now return to the monkeyflowers. The red one grows mainly at lower elevations, the pink one higher up. Their flowers suit different pollinators.
scenes.visual: The hillside from the first film: RED flowers low with a HUMMINGBIRD, PINK flowers high with a BUMBLEBEE. An elevation arrow on the side labelled 'higher'.
scenes.narration: Now return to the monkeyflowers. The red one grows mainly at lower elevations, the pink one higher up. Their flowers suit different pollinators.

scenes.tts: The pink flower is wide, with a small nectar reward, and bumblebees visit it. The red flower has a narrow tube and a large reward, and hummingbirds visit it.
scenes.visual: Close-ups side by side: PINK wide flower with a small nectar drop, bumblebee landing; RED narrow-tubed flower with a large nectar drop, hummingbird hovering. Cartoon flowers, schematic.
scenes.narration: The pink flower is wide, with a small nectar reward, and bumblebees visit it. The red flower has a narrow tube and a large reward, and hummingbirds visit it.

scenes.tts: Those adaptations are themselves the gates. Plants adapted to different elevations rarely meet. A pollinator that favours one flower carries little pollen to the other.
scenes.visual: The adapted traits morph into the first film's GREY gates: the elevation arrow becomes the 'habitat' gate, the two flowers with their pollinators become the 'pollinator' gate. The GOLD stream thins through both.
scenes.narration: Those adaptations are themselves the gates. Plants adapted to different elevations rarely meet. A pollinator that favours one flower carries little pollen to the other.

scenes.tts: Fish or flowers, the lesson is the same. Adapt to different places and partners, and isolation often grows as a side effect.
scenes.visual: Split screen: OLIVE and SILVER-BLUE fish apart in a lake; PINK and RED flowers apart on the hillside. A single GREY gate between each pair.
scenes.narration: Fish or flowers, the lesson is the same. Adapt to different places and partners, and isolation often grows as a side effect.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex, the hexagon mascot, wearing a tiny snorkel. Line: 'Adapt to different habitats, and isolation often follows as a side effect.'
